title: The Nuniyya of al-Rundi
intro: Abu al-Baqa' al-Rundi wrote this elegy, named the Nuniyya for its rhyme in nun, for the cities of al-Andalus that fell to the Christian kingdoms in the seventh century AH (the thirteenth CE), from Valencia, Murcia, Xativa and Jaen to Cordoba and Seville, and as a call for help to the Muslims across the sea. The Marinid chronicle al-Dhakhira al-Saniyya says he composed it when Ibn al-Ahmar, the ruler of Granada, handed a number of towns to the king of Castile in 665 AH (1267 CE). It opens on the passing of all things and of the great kings and peoples of the past, then mourns the cities of the Peninsula and their mosques turned into churches, calls on the horsemen beyond the sea, and ends with the captives: a mother parted from her child, a girl led away by her captor. Al-Maqqari, who gives it in Nafh al-Tib and Azhar al-Riyad, warns that copies in circulation add lines on Granada, Baza and other cities taken after the poet's death, and says he copied his own text from the handwriting of a trustworthy man. The historian Muhammad Abdallah Inan counts it among the finest and most moving of national elegies.

translation: Everything, once it reaches its fullness, begins to wane,
so let no one be deceived by the sweetness of life.
1.sharh: Whatever reaches completion starts to decline: that is the rule of the world. So no one should let an easy, pleasant life deceive him, for fullness is where loss begins. The maxim prepares the lament to come.

translation: Affairs, as you have seen, pass from hand to hand:
whom one season pleases, many seasons grieve.
2.sharh: Fortunes change hands, as anyone who has watched them knows, and one good season is paid for with many bad ones. The second half is word for word the second half of a line in al-Busti's Nuniyya, in the same metre and rhyme; al-Zirikli notes that lines of the two poems have become mixed.

translation: This abode spares no one,
and nothing of hers stays in one state.
3.sharh: The world, called here simply “this abode”, spares no one, and none of its affairs holds steady. Change is its nature, and nothing in it lasts; the following lines show this in the fate of arms and kings.

translation: Time is bound to tear through every coat of mail
even when swords and spears glance off it.
4.sharh: Armour that no sword or spear could pierce still wears through in the end. Time accomplishes what weapons cannot, so no defence a man can buy protects him from it.

translation: It draws every sword for destruction, even were the sword
Ibn Dhi Yazan himself, and Ghumdan its sheath.
5.sharh: Every sword time draws to kill is itself drawn to be destroyed, as Abdallah al-Tayyib explains. The pun rests on names: the Yemeni king was Sayf, “sword”, ibn Dhi Yazan, and Ghumdan, the palace said to be his, sounds like ghimd, “sheath”.

translation: Where are the crowned kings of Yemen,
and where are their diadems and crowns?
6.sharh: The first of the poem's questions beginning “where are”, asked of the vanished kings. It starts with the crowned kings of Yemen and their regalia; the answer, left unsaid, is that nothing of them remains.

translation: Where is what Shaddad raised in Iram,
and what Sasan ruled among the Persians?
7.sharh: The questions move to legendary builders and rulers: Shaddad, who raised Iram, and Sasan, whose house ruled Persia. Their buildings and their realms are both gone. Sasahu, “he ruled it”, echoes the name Sasan.

translation: Where is the gold that Qarun amassed,
and where are Ad, Adnan and Qahtan?
8.sharh: Wealth goes the way of power: Qarun's hoard has gone, and so have whole peoples, Ad and the first ancestors of the Arabs. Neither riches nor ancient lineage escapes the common end.

translation: Upon them all came a decree none can turn back,
until they were gone, as if they had never been.
9.sharh: This answers the string of questions: a fate no one can avert overtook all of them, and they vanished so completely that it is as though they never existed.

translation: All they had of kingship, and all their kings,
became like the dream a drowsy sleeper tells.
10.sharh: Kingdoms and kings alike have turned into a dream retold on waking, vivid and unreal. Mulk, “kingship”, and malik, “king”, differ only in their vowels. Al-Tayyib finds here a true picture of the party kings of al-Andalus.

translation: Time turned on Dara and on his killer,
and sought out Kisra, whom his palace could not shelter.
11.sharh: Time destroyed the Persian king Dara and Alexander, who brought him down, vanquished and victor alike, and its blow found Kisra, whose great hall could not protect him. Dara echoes dara, “turned”.

translation: As though no way had ever opened for al-Sa'b,
and Solomon had never ruled the world.
12.sharh: Even the mightiest are as though they had never been: al-Sa'b, to whom every way lay open, and Solomon, whose kingdom was the world. Sa'b means “hard” and yashul “to come easily”, a contrast the translation loses.

translation: The blows of time are of many kinds,
and time brings joys and sorrows.
13.sharh: Calamity takes many forms, and time deals out gladness as well as grief. The commonplace prepares the next line, which sets one calamity apart from all the others.

translation: Every misfortune has some comfort to ease it,
but what has befallen Islam has none.
14.sharh: Time heals ordinary losses, but nothing can console the loss that Islam has suffered. Here the poem turns from the common fate of kings to its real subject, the loss of Muslim al-Andalus.

translation: A blow has struck the Peninsula past all consoling:
Uhud fell at it, and Thahlan crumbled.
15.sharh: The disaster that has struck al-Andalus, the Peninsula, is beyond comfort; mountains would collapse under it. Al-Tayyib reads the two mountains as symbols: Uhud for Islam, Thahlan for the Arabs.

translation: The evil eye struck her in her Islam, and she was tried
until whole regions and cities were empty of it.
16.sharh: The loss is pictured as the work of the evil eye, as if al-Andalus had been envied for its faith. The trial went on until Islam had vanished from region after region and city after city.

translation: Ask Valencia what has become of Murcia,
and where Xativa is, or where Jaen.
17.sharh: The roll call of lost cities begins. The listener is told to ask one fallen city about another, as if Valencia could answer for Murcia; none can, for all of them are in Christian hands.

translation: Where is Cordoba, the home of learning,
where so many scholars rose to eminence?
18.sharh: Cordoba is mourned for what it gave to learning: the long line of scholars who rose to eminence there. With it al-Andalus loses not only a city but its centre of knowledge.

translation: Where is Hims, and all the gardens it held,
and its sweet river, brimming and full?
19.sharh: Seville is called here by its Andalusian name, Hims, and remembered for its pleasure gardens and its river running full. Al-Tayyib notes that a brimming river is worth praising in a land whose rivers shrink in the dry season.

translation: They were capitals, the pillars of the land,
and what can last once the pillars are gone?
20.sharh: These cities were the main seats of al-Andalus, the pillars that held the whole building up. With them gone, nothing that remains can hope to stand. Al-baqa', “survival”, and tabqa, “remain”, share a root.

translation: The pure Hanifi faith weeps for grief,
as a lovesick man weeps when parted from his dearest,
21.sharh: Islam itself is pictured as a mourner, grieving like a lover parted from the one he loves. The loss belongs not only to the people of al-Andalus but to their faith.

translation: for homes of Islam left empty,
deserted, though unbelief has filled them,
22.sharh: The towns are full of people, yet to the poet they are a wasteland, because Islam has left them. Al-Tayyib hears an echo of the Quran: “only he maintains God's mosques who believes in God” (9:18).

translation: where the mosques have become churches,
holding nothing but bells and crosses.
23.sharh: Inside the converted mosques the signs of Islam are gone, replaced by the bell that calls to Christian prayer and the cross. The line sets what the mosques were against what they have become.

translation: Even the prayer niches weep, lifeless as they are;
even the pulpits mourn, though they are only wood.
24.sharh: Grief has spread even to things without life, the prayer niche of stone and the pulpit of wood. Al-Tayyib traces the image to the palm trunk that, in the hadith, moaned when the Prophet left it.

translation: You heedless one, to whom time offers a lesson:
if you are dozing, time is wide awake.
25.sharh: The poem turns to those who still feel safe. Time is full of warnings for anyone who will heed them; whoever sleeps through them will find that time does not sleep, and that what befell others will come to him.

translation: And you who stroll at ease, absorbed in your homeland:
after Hims, can any homeland still deceive a man?
26.sharh: Addressed to those whose cities are still safe, the people of Granada among them, as al-Tayyib reads it. If Seville could fall, no home is secure, and to trust in one is self-deception.

translation: That calamity has blotted out all that came before it,
and however long time runs it will not be forgotten.
27.sharh: The loss of al-Andalus outweighs every earlier disaster, which now seems small beside it. Time, which wears other griefs away, will never wear this one away. Ansat, “made forget”, and nisyan, “forgetting”, share a root.

translation: You who ride lean thoroughbred horses
that race like eagles on the course,
28.sharh: The appeal begins. The poet calls on the horsemen across the sea in North Africa, praising their fine, lean horses that fly like eagles, before asking why they have not ridden to help.

translation: you who carry keen Indian swords
that blaze like fire in the darkness of the dust,
29.sharh: He praises their arms: Indian swords, thin-edged and keen, flashing like fire through the cloud of dust that battle raises. The praise is pointed, for these are the very means of rescue.

translation: you who live at ease across the sea,
mighty and sovereign in your own lands:
30.sharh: The people beyond the sea live in comfort and security, with power of their own. The poet sets their ease against the fate of al-Andalus to shame them into answering.

translation: have you news of the people of al-Andalus?
Riders have carried their story far and wide.
31.sharh: The question is a reproach. Travellers have carried the news everywhere, so the people beyond the sea cannot claim not to know, and nothing excuses their staying at home.

translation: How often the helpless cry to us for help,
slain and captive, and no one stirs.
32.sharh: The weak of al-Andalus, killed or taken captive, keep calling on the Muslim world, and no one moves. The word for “the helpless” recalls the Quran's call to fight for “the oppressed men, women and children” (4:75).

translation: What is this estrangement among you in Islam,
when you, servants of God, are brothers?
33.sharh: A reproach to the Muslim rulers for their quarrels and divisions. Brothers in faith should not stand apart from one another, least of all while their own people in al-Andalus are being destroyed.

translation: Are there no proud souls with high resolve?
Has goodness no helpers and supporters?
34.sharh: He longs for men too proud to accept humiliation and asks whether goodness has no one left to fight for it. The question is a summons: it calls on its hearers to be those helpers.

translation: Who will pity a people brought low after their glory,
their state overturned by tyranny and oppression?
35.sharh: A cry of pity for the Muslims of al-Andalus, humbled after their days of power, their condition overturned by injustice and tyranny. The poet asks who will take pity on them, and the question is itself a call for help.

translation: Yesterday they were kings in their own homes;
today they are slaves in the lands of unbelief.
36.sharh: The contrast carries the whole tragedy: masters of their own houses yesterday, slaves in Christian lands today. Each half answers the other, yesterday against today and kings against slaves.

translation: If you could see them, bewildered, with no one to guide them,
dressed in every colour of humiliation,
37.sharh: The listener is asked to picture the captives: lost, with no one to lead them, wearing their humiliation as plainly as clothes. Its “colours” are its many kinds.

translation: and if you saw them weeping as they are sold,
the sight would terrify you and grief would carry you off.
38.sharh: The captives are sold as slaves, and their weeping at the sale would horrify anyone who saw it. Istahwatka, “carried you off”, is the Quran's word for a man led astray by devils (6:71), as al-Tayyib notes, so this grief is close to madness.

translation: How many a mother and child have been torn apart,
as souls are parted from bodies,
39.sharh: Families are broken up at the sale, a mother sold one way and her child another, never to meet again. The poet likens it to death itself, the parting of soul and body.

translation: and many a young girl, lovely as the sun at its rising,
as though she were rubies and coral,
40.sharh: The girl is described in the Quran's words for the maidens of paradise, “as though they were rubies and coral” (55:58), as al-Tayyib points out. Her purity makes what follows all the more terrible.

translation: dragged by the brute to what she dreads, against her will,
her eyes weeping, her heart bewildered.
41.sharh: The girl is led away by her captor to be violated, unable to resist. Al-Tayyib explains her bewilderment: she had been sheltered all her life, and now captivity has brought her to this.

translation: At such things the heart melts with grief,
if there is any Islam and faith in it.
42.sharh: The poem ends on a challenge: anyone who truly believes must be heartbroken by such things, so grief for al-Andalus becomes a test of faith. The reciter says the closing line twice, the second time softly.

2.1.5.head: دُوَل
2.1.5.meaning: Duwal: things that pass in turn from one party to another.

4.1.5.head: سابِغَة
4.1.5.meaning: Sabigha: a long, full coat of mail.

4.2.2.head: نَبا
4.2.2.meaning: Glanced off without cutting, said of a sword.

4.2.3.head: مَشرَفِيّات
4.2.3.meaning: Mashrafi swords, named after al-Masharif, villages of Arabia near the farmland.

4.2.4.head: خُرصان
4.2.4.meaning: Spears. The reciter says khursan, as Nafh al-Tib prints it; Lisan al-Arab gives the plural as khirsan.

5.2.2-4.meaning: Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, a king of Yemen who freed his country from Abyssinian rule.

5.2.6.head: غُمدان
5.2.6.meaning: Ghumdan: a famous palace in Yemen, said to have been the domed hall of Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan.

6.2.3.head: أَكاليل
6.2.3.meaning: Diadems: bands set with jewels; a crown is also called iklil.

7.1.4.head: شَدّاد
7.1.4.meaning: Shaddad son of Ad, to whom the building of Iram of the Pillars is credited.

7.1.6.head: إِرَم
7.1.6.meaning: Iram “of the pillars”, named in the Quran with the people of Ad (89:7); some took it for a tribe, others for a city.

7.2.6.head: ساسان
7.2.6.meaning: Sasan: the ancestor of the house of Sasan, the Persian kings called Kisra.

8.1.4.head: قارون
8.1.4.meaning: Qarun: Korah, of the people of Moses, whose treasure the Quran describes; the earth swallowed him and his house (28:76–81).

8.2.2.head: عاد
8.2.2.meaning: Ad: the people of the prophet Hud, destroyed by a howling wind (Quran 69:6).

8.2.3.head: عَدنان
8.2.3.meaning: Adnan: father of Ma'add, an early ancestor of the Arabs. The editions have Shaddad.

8.2.4.head: قَحطان
8.2.4.meaning: Qahtan: the forefather of the Yemenis.

10.2.6.head: وَسنان
10.2.6.meaning: Wasnan: a sleeper not yet deep in sleep.

11.1.4.meaning: Dara: Darius, the Persian king whom Alexander defeated; al-Tabari says that when his army broke, two of his own guards stabbed him.

11.1.5.head: قاتِل
11.1.5.meaning: His killer: Alexander, whom the classical authors call “the killer of Dara”; al-Jahiz reports that when he died a Persian sage said, “I never thought the killer of Dara would die.” Azhar al-Riyad reads qatalahu, “fought him”.

11.2.2.meaning: Kisra: Chosroes, the title of the Persian kings.

11.2.5.head: إيوان
11.2.5.meaning: Iwan: the great vaulted hall of Kisra at al-Mada'in (Ctesiphon).

12.1.2.head: الصَّعب
12.1.2.meaning: Al-Sa'b ibn Dhi Marathid, a king of Himyar whom Yemeni tradition identifies with Dhu al-Qarnayn of the Quran.

12.2.5.head: سُلَيمان
12.2.5.meaning: Solomon, who asked God for a kingdom such as no one after him would have (Quran 38:35).

14.1.2.head: سُلوان
14.1.2.meaning: Sulwan: what consoles and eases grief.

15.1.2.head: الجَزيرة
15.1.2.meaning: “The Peninsula”: al-Andalus, as its people called it.

15.2.5.head: ثَهلان
15.2.5.meaning: Thahlan: a massive mountain in Najd.

16.1.2.head: العَين
16.1.2.meaning: The evil eye: harm from an envious look.

16.1.5.head: اِمتَحَنَ
16.1.5.meaning: She was put to the trial. Azhar al-Riyad reads irtuzi'at, “she was bereaved”.

17.1.2.head: بَلَنسِيَة
17.1.2.meaning: Balansiya: Valencia, taken by the Christians in 636 AH (1238 CE).

17.1.5.head: مُرسِيَة
17.1.5.meaning: Mursiya: Murcia, which submitted to Castile in 640 AH (1243 CE) and was taken by Aragon in 664 AH (1266 CE).

17.2.2.head: شاطِبَة
17.2.2.meaning: Shatiba: Xativa, a large city in eastern al-Andalus, known for its paper, taken by Aragon in 644 AH (1246 CE); the Quran reader al-Shatibi came from it.

17.2.5.head: جَيّان
17.2.5.meaning: Jayyan: Jaen, handed to Castile in 643 AH (1246 CE); the grammarian Ibn Malik came from it.

18.1.2.head: قُرطُبَة
18.1.2.meaning: Qurtuba: Cordoba, the old caliphal capital, taken by Castile in 633 AH (1236 CE).

19.1.2.head: حِمص
19.1.2.meaning: Hims: Seville, named after Homs in Syria, whose soldiers settled it; taken by Castile in 646 AH (1248 CE).

20.1.1.head: قَواعِد
20.1.1.meaning: Qawa'id: chief cities; literally the foundations of a building.

21.1.2-3.meaning: “The pure Hanifi faith”: Islam, the religion of Abraham the hanif; bayda', “white”, means clear and spotless.

21.2.5.head: هَيمان
21.2.5.meaning: Hayman: distraught with love; originally, maddened by thirst.

23.2.3.head: نَواقيس
23.2.3.meaning: Nawaqis: what Christians strike to call the faithful to prayer; here, church bells.

24.1.2.head: المَحاريب
24.1.2.meaning: Mihrabs: the niches in the wall of a mosque that mark the direction of prayer.

25.2.4.head: سِنَة
25.2.4.meaning: Sina: drowsiness, the first touch of sleep, as in the Quran's “neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him” (2:255).

26.1.2.head: مَرِح
26.1.2.meaning: Exultant past all measure, as in the Quran's “do not walk the earth exultantly” (17:37).

28.1.3.head: عِتاق
28.1.3.meaning: Itaq: thoroughbreds, the finest of their kind.

28.2.5.head: عِقبان
28.2.5.meaning: Iqban: eagles, birds of prey known for their swoop.

29.2.4.head: النَّقع
29.2.4.meaning: Naq': the dust that rises over a battle.

30.1.1.head: راتِع
30.1.1.meaning: Rati'in: living at ease, like herds grazing on rich pasture.

30.1.2-3.meaning: “Across the sea”: North Africa, facing al-Andalus over the strait.

32.1.4.head: المُستَضعَفون
32.1.4.meaning: The oppressed, too weak to defend themselves.

35.2.3.head: جَور
35.2.3.meaning: Jawr: tyranny, injustice. The editions have kufr, “unbelief”.

38.2.3.head: اِستَهوى
38.2.3.meaning: Carried you off, robbed you of your wits.

40.2.4.head: مَرجان
40.2.4.meaning: Marjan: small pearls, as most lexicographers have it, or red coral.

41.1.2.head: العِلج
41.1.2.meaning: Ilj: a burly unbeliever of the non-Arabs; here, the Christian captor.

42.1.6.head: كَمَد
42.1.6.meaning: Kamad: grief kept hidden, or grief at its worst.
